etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English scho, sho, from Old English sċōh (“shoe”), from Proto-West Germanic *skōh, from Proto-Germanic *skōhaz (“shoe”), of unclear etymology; possibly a derivation from *skehaną (“to move quickly”), from Proto-Indo-European *skek- (“to move quickly, jump”). Eclipsed non-native Middle English sabatine, sabatoun (“shoe”) from Medieval Latin sabatēnum, sabatum (“shoe, slipper”) (compare Old Occitan sabatō, Spanish zapato (“shoe”), French sabot (“wooden shoe, clog”), Italian ciabatta). The archaic plural shoon is from Middle English shon, from Old English scōn, scōum (“shoes”, dative plural) and scōna (“shoes'”, genitive plural); it is cognate with Scots shuin (“shoes”).

definitions.definition: (footwear) A protective covering for the foot, with a bottom part composed of thick leather or plastic sole and often a thicker heel, and a softer upper part made of leather or synthetic material. Shoes generally do not extend above the ankle, as opposed to boots, which do.
A piece of metal designed to be attached to a horse's foot as a means of protection; a horseshoe.
(card games) A device for holding multiple decks of playing cards, allowing more games to be played by reducing the time between shuffles.
A band of iron or steel, or a ship of wood, fastened to the bottom of the runner of a sleigh, or any vehicle which slides on the snow.
A drag, or sliding piece of wood or iron, placed under the wheel of a loaded vehicle, to retard its motion in going down a hill.
The part of a railroad car brake which presses upon the wheel to retard its motion.
(architecture) A trough-shaped or spout-shaped member, put at the bottom of the water leader coming from the eaves gutter, so as to throw the water off from the building.
A trough or spout for conveying grain from the hopper to the eye of the millstone.
An inclined trough in an ore-crushing mill.
An iron socket or plate to take the thrust of a strut or rafter.
An iron socket to protect the point of a wooden pile.
(engineering) A plate, or notched piece, interposed between a moving part and the stationary part on which it bears, to take the wear and afford means of adjustment; called also slipper and gib.
Part of a current collector on electric trains which provides contact either with a live rail or an overhead wire (fitted to a pantograph in the latter case).
(historical) An ingot of gold or silver shaped somewhat like a traditional Chinese shoe, formerly used in trade in the Far East.

quote.citation: 1806, Lawrence Dundas Campbell, E. Samuel, The Asiatic Annual Register, page 56:
quote.text: The finest gold among them is 100 touch, called Sycee, i. e. pure gold without alloy: so that if a shoe of gold touch 93, then it hath 93 parts of fine gold and 7 parts alloy.

definitions.definition: Something resembling a shoe in form, position, or function, such as a brake shoe.
The outer cover or tread of a pneumatic tire, especially for an automobile.
(by extension, slang) A pneumatic tire, especially for an automobile.
(slang) A fake passport.
(intransitive) To put shoes on one's own feet.
(transitive) To put shoes on someone or something else's feet, especially to put horseshoes on a horse.

quote.citation: 1874, Thomas Hardy, chapter XXXII, in Far from the Madding Crowd:
quote.text: "Old Jimmy Harris only shoed her last week, and I'd swear to his make among ten thousand."

definitions.definition: (intransitive, chiefly as past participle) To cover an object with a protective layer of material.

quote.citation: 1930, Sax Rohmer, The Day the World Ended, published 1969, page iv. 38:
quote.text: And they had been made by the same brand of tire as that which shod the car I sat in!
